analysis.one_liner: Bans flavored e-cigarettes, raises federal tobacco taxes to cigarette-level rates, and tightens online sales rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in three House committees for two years and drew zero cosponsors before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would fight youth vaping three ways. It would ban kid-appealing flavors like mango, mint, and candy in e-cigarettes and other non-cigarette tobacco products, unless a maker proves to the FDA that a flavor helps smokers quit. It would raise federal excise taxes on cigars, pipe tobacco, and chewing tobacco to match the cigarette tax, tax e-cigarettes at cigarette-equivalent rates, and index all tobacco taxes to inflation. It would also extend a federal reporting law so online and mail-order sellers of e-cigarettes must tell states where their shipments go, closing a loophole that made it cheap and easy for minors to buy vapes online.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teens, who face the sharpest rise in nicotine addiction: the CDC's youth survey found high-school e-cigarette use had roughly tripled in a year, and the bill's findings cite a study where nearly 94% of teens in a test successfully bought e-cigarettes online because sites lacked age checks. Parents and schools also benefit from fewer flavored products marketed to kids. State and local governments would collect more of the tobacco taxes they are already owed, since online sellers currently bypass them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Teens and young people at risk of addiction

how_it_helps.text: Bans characterizing flavors — including menthol, fruit, candy, and dessert flavors — in e-cigarettes and other non-cigarette tobacco products, unless the FDA finds a manufacturer proved the flavor helps smokers quit, does not appeal to youth, and does not add harm [S3].

Raises the federal excise tax on pipe and roll-your-own tobacco to $24.78 per pound, on smokeless tobacco to $13.42 per pound, and on large cigars to $24.78 per pound — roughly matching the cigarette tax rate instead of today's far lower rates — and taxes any FDA-regulated tobacco product, including e-cigarettes, at a cigarette-equivalent rate [S3].
Requires tobacco taxes to rise with inflation each year, so the tax does not erode in real terms over time [S3].

Extends the Jenkins Act so online and mail-order sellers must report e-cigarette shipments — customer names, addresses, and quantities — to state tax officials, making it harder for minors and tax-dodging sellers to operate over the internet [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Adults who use e-cigarettes, cigars, chewing tobacco, or pipe tobacco would pay significantly higher prices, because excise taxes are passed through to the shelf price. Manufacturers of those products — especially e-cigarette companies, whose flavors and low-taxed prices drive much of their sales — would lose revenue or exit the market. Online tobacco retailers would bear new reporting costs and lose the anonymity that made internet sales easy.
analysis.who_pays_short: E-cigarette and cigar makers, adult tobacco users

drawbacks.text: The new excise taxes land on all users, not just minors. Tobacco taxes are regressive — they take a larger share of income from lower-income adult smokers and vapers, who would pay the new rates whether or not they ever bought products for a teenager [S3].

The flavor ban covers menthol in e-cigarettes, removing the flavor many adult smokers use when switching away from cigarettes. Critics of flavor bans argue this can push adults back to cigarettes rather than off nicotine, and the bill only permits flavors a manufacturer can affirmatively prove to the FDA aid cessation [S3].

The cigar and pipe provisions also raise prices for a small but real group of lower-volume adult users, and the tax on 'other tobacco products' delegates the exact e-cigarette rate to Treasury rulemaking, leaving final costs uncertain at passage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong: the bill targets the specific mechanisms — candy and fruit flavors, cheap untaxed internet sales — that drove teen e-cigarette use from under 5% to over 13% of high schoolers in about a year, according to the findings in the bill text. The honest cost is that the tax increases hit adult users, including lower-income ones, and the menthol and flavor restrictions may complicate switching for adult smokers. On balance the bill is designed to price and format tobacco so it stops appealing to children, with the burden falling mainly on the industries selling to them and on adults who choose to keep using the products.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees, then to two subcommittees, and no committee ever held a hearing or voted to send it to the floor before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on January 8, 2019, the opening day of the 116th Congress [S1].
The House referred it to three committees — Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce — meaning no single panel owned the bill [S5].
The bill was referred to Health subcommittees in both the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees in early 2019, and no action of any kind followed [S5].
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor at any point in the two-year Congress [S4].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the bill never having received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: E-cigarette, cigar, and smokeless tobacco companies are better off: they kept the existing low federal tax rates, kept flavored products on the market, and online sellers kept the reporting loophole. No youth-prevention benefit was ever delivered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Vaping and tobacco makers kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 116th Congress and served as its only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: First committee of referral; held no hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on day one, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never reported the bill out or scheduled any action on it for two years.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tobacco product standards
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, assigned it to its Health Subcommittee, and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No other member of either party cosponsored the bill and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no measurable partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would ban the fruit, candy, mint, and dessert flavors that drive most youth-appealing sales and tax vaping products at cigarette-equivalent federal rates. Its business model depended on both staying unchanged, so its interest ran directly against the bill's youth-protection goal.
Large cigars are currently taxed as a percentage of manufacturer price; the bill would switch them to $24.78 per pound, a major cost increase for premium and discount cigar makers alike.

The bill would raise the smokeless tobacco tax roughly nine-fold to $13.42 per pound and pipe tobacco to cigarette parity, and extend taxes to dissolvable nicotine products sold as lozenges or pouches.

Extending the Jenkins Act reporting requirement to e-cigarettes would force internet sellers to disclose shipments to state tax authorities, ending the anonymity and uncollected state taxes that made online sales cheap for minors to exploit.
States and cities that tax tobacco would collect revenue currently bypassed through internet sales, and gain a new enforcement tool for youth access laws.
